summary: This standards-track document defines the MIME Multipart/Related content type, a common way to represent an object made of several related body parts, with examples of its use. It was replaced by RFC 2387.

plainLanguage.summary: A box holding a main page plus its pictures, all labeled as belonging together.

questions: how to package html and images in email
how do i send html with images in email
how do compound mime objects work
how do mime parts reference each other
subtitle: A standard way to send related documents together, like HTML with its images.

tldr.problem: Email and document systems need a standard way to represent a compound object made of several pieces that reference each other, such as a web page with embedded images.
tldr.mechanism: Multipart/Related defines a MIME container with a type parameter (the media type of the root), a start parameter (pointing to the main part), and optional start-info (auxiliary data), allowing all parts to be packaged and transmitted as a single entity.
tldr.outcome: Authors can reliably send structured documents with embedded resources without ambiguity about which part is the root or how parts relate; it was later refined by RFC 2387.

today: RFC 2112 is Proposed Standard status and has been obsoleted by RFC 2387, which refines the definition. Modern email and web systems use Multipart/Related when sending structured documents with embedded resources.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2112 defines the Multipart/Related MIME content-type, a mechanism for representing compound objects made of multiple inter-related body parts. Such objects include web pages with embedded images, spreadsheets with external references, or other documents where the constituent parts make sense only together.

The RFC addresses a practical problem: earlier MIME specifications either lacked a general mechanism for such aggregates or required a new specific subtype for each new kind of compound object. Multipart/Related provides a single, reusable framework where the type parameter specifies what kind of object is being transmitted, and the start parameter designates the root part.
sections.plainLanguage: When you want to send an HTML page with its images as one package, you need a standard way to say 'these parts belong together' and 'start with this part first'. This standard provides that.

sections.title: The Multipart/Related Structure
sections.content:
A Multipart/Related message consists of a container with required and optional parameters followed by multiple body parts.

The type parameter is mandatory and specifies the MIME media type of the root part (for example, text/html or application/xhtml+xml). This lets the recipient determine the object type without inspecting the enclosed parts.

The start parameter optionally points to a content-ID identifying the root part—the part the application should process first. If start is not given, the first body part in the message is the root.

The start-info parameter provides auxiliary information that may be needed when unpacking or processing the object, such as command-line options or references to another body part. Its interpretation depends on the application.
sections.plainLanguage: You label the container with what type of object it is. You tell it which part is the main one (by default it's the first). You can include extra instructions for how to process it.

sections.title: Body Part Relationships
sections.content:
Within a Multipart/Related structure, body parts reference each other using content-IDs. A content-ID is a unique identifier assigned to each part that other parts can reference via URLs of the form cid:<content-id>.

For example, an HTML document might include <img src='cid:<picture@example.com>'> to reference an image body part. This approach keeps all related resources within the same message and avoids external URL lookups.

Multipart/Related processing takes precedence over Content-Disposition headers (which suggest inline or attachment handling). A Multipart/Related-aware application controls the presentation and ignores disposition hints, since the compound object's internal structure already defines how parts relate.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part gets an ID number. Parts can say 'show me the picture with ID 42' by referencing that ID. The application knows how to arrange them all together, so it ignores old-style 'show inline' hints.

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content:
One common use is sending an HTML document with embedded images. The root part contains markup that references image parts by content-ID. An X-Okie example in the RFC shows a text/x-Okie document with two images referenced by cid: URLs, all packaged together so a mail client can display the complete document without fetching external resources.

Another example is a fixed-record format document: the root part (type application/x-FixedRecord) contains record lengths as ASCII text, and a separate body part contains binary data. The record lengths tell the application how to parse the binary part.

The RFC notes that such objects may be stored locally, and when stored, the receiving application or a specialized receiving agent may need to convert the content-ID references to local file names or process the parts in other application-specific ways.
sections.plainLanguage: You could send a website as one email: the HTML file says 'include my picture ID 1, my style sheet ID 2, etc.' and all those pieces come with it. Or you could send a data file with a separate record-length table.

sections.title: User Agent Handling
sections.content:
Mail user agents that recognize Multipart/Related must gather all constituent parts, identify the root (using the start parameter or defaulting to the first part), and pass all parts to the application that handles the object's type.

Critically, the application—not the mail client—is responsible for interpreting the relationships and rendering or processing the compound object. The mail client's job is to extract and deliver the parts intact.

Agents that do not recognize Multipart/Related should treat it as Multipart/Mixed (a simple collection of parts) for compatibility. This graceful degradation ensures that older systems can at least access individual parts, even if they cannot reconstruct the compound object correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: A modern email client reads 'this is Multipart/Related' and passes all the pieces to the application that knows how to use them. An old client doesn't understand and just shows them as separate attachments.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 2112 states that security considerations for Multipart/Related are identical to those of the underlying content-type. The Multipart/Related wrapper itself does not introduce new security risks or guarantees.

Security implications depend on the type of the root part: a text/html document may be vulnerable to script injection, while a proprietary binary format may have its own parsing risks. Applications must validate and safely process the contained parts according to the security model of their type.
sections.plainLanguage: If you trust the HTML format, you trust Multipart/Related HTML. If you don't trust the binary format inside, Multipart/Related doesn't change that. Security depends on what the actual content is.
